title: Quiz: Robust Regression and Generalised Additive Models

questions.text: In robust regression with Huber's M-estimator, how are large residuals treated compared to OLS?
options: Large residuals are excluded completely from the loss calculation
Large residuals are squared, just like in OLS
Large residuals are assigned linear (not quadratic) weight, reducing their influence
Large residuals are replaced by their absolute value before squaring
questions.explanation: The Huber loss is quadratic for small residuals (|r| ≤ k) but linear for large residuals (|r| > k). This caps the influence of outliers — they contribute linearly, not quadratically.

questions.text: In a GAM, edf = 1.0 for a smooth term s(x) means the relationship between x and y is estimated to be perfectly linear.
questions.explanation: edf = 1 means the smooth degenerates to a straight line — mgcv estimated that no non-linearity is needed. You can replace s(x) with the linear term x without loss of fit.

questions.text: When would you prefer MASS::rlm() over lm()?
options: When you need p-values for the coefficients
When the residuals contain a few large outliers that may not represent the bulk of the data
When the response variable is binary
When the model has more than 10 predictors
questions.explanation: rlm() is designed for situations where some observations have unusually large residuals (outliers or contaminated data). By down-weighting large residuals, it produces estimates that reflect the bulk of the data.

questions.text: In mgcv::gam(), what does te(x1, x2) do differently from s(x1) + s(x2)?
options: te() fits separate linear models for x1 and x2
te() estimates a 2D interaction surface; s(x1) + s(x2) assumes the effects are additive
te() requires x1 and x2 to be categorical variables
te() forces edf = 1 for both x1 and x2
questions.explanation: s(x1) + s(x2) is an additive model: the effect of x1 on y is the same regardless of x2 (and vice versa). te(x1, x2) fits a tensor-product smooth — a full 2D surface that allows the effect of x1 to depend on x2.

questions.text: method = 'REML' in gam() is preferred over method = 'ML' because:
options: REML is faster to compute for large datasets
REML produces less biased estimates of the smoothness parameters, reducing overfitting
REML allows the model to have more knots
REML is the only method that supports te() tensor smooths
questions.explanation: Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) treats the smoothness parameters as variance components and estimates them more accurately than ML, which tends to undersmooth (overfit). REML is the recommended default in mgcv.
